turns.learner: I'm 15. Why is the sky blue and not violet?
turns.reply:
Sunlight contains all colors, but the atmosphere scatters blue light much more than red, making the sky look blue. Violet is scattered even more, but our eyes are less sensitive to it, and some violet is absorbed high up. 

If our eyes were as sensitive to violet as to blue, and there was less absorption, what color do you think the sky would look?

turns.learner: ok
turns.reply:
If our eyes detected violet as strongly as blue, the sky would actually appear violet, since violet light is scattered even more! Let's move on to how this scattering works.

What do you think would happen to the sky’s color if the atmosphere scattered all colors of light equally?

turns.learner: Because blue is the strongest light from the sun?
turns.reply: Sunlight actually contains all the colors, not just blue. Imagine if all those colors were scattered equally—what would that make the sky look like?

turns.learner: um, something about the air maybe?
turns.reply:
Air itself has no color; it just scatters sunlight. If all colors were scattered equally, the sky would look white, like sunlight itself. The reason we see blue is because blue is scattered a lot more than other colors.

Now, let’s focus on the effects of our eyes and the ozone layer. How do you think the ozone layer and our eye sensitivity affect whether we see more blue or more violet in the sky?

turns.learner: Shorter wavelengths like blue and violet scatter more off air molecules.
turns.reply:
The ozone layer absorbs much of the violet light before it gets to your eyes, and our eyes are better at seeing blue than violet. That’s why the sky looks blue instead of violet.

Can you sum up, in your own words, why the sky isn’t violet even though violet light is scattered more?

turns.learner: continue
turns.reply:
The sky isn’t violet because, even though violet light scatters more, the ozone layer absorbs most violet and our eyes can’t see it well—so blue dominates.

Would you like to know why sunsets look red or orange next, or do you have a question about sky color?

turns.learner: ok
turns.reply:
The ozone layer absorbs most violet light, and our eyes are much less sensitive to violet than blue. Even though violet is scattered more, these two effects make the sky appear blue instead.

If Earth’s air scattered red light the most (instead of blue and violet), what color would the midday sky look?

turns.learner: Our eyes are more sensitive to blue than violet, and sunlight has less violet.
turns.reply:
That’s not quite it. If the air scattered red light the most, the sky would look red during the day, because the color that is scattered most is what fills the sky.

Suppose you were on a planet where the air scattered green light more than any other color—what color would the sky appear there?

Now, what do you think happens if your body meets the same virus years later?

turns.learner: I'm 16. How do supply and demand set a price?
turns.reply: I couldn't reach the tutor model just now. Please try asking again in a moment.

turns.learner: ok
turns.reply:
Supply is how much sellers want to sell, and demand is how much buyers want to buy at different prices. The price is set where these two meet—called the equilibrium price. 

What do you think happens if sellers want to sell more than buyers want to buy at a certain price?

turns.learner: Sellers just pick whatever price they want?
turns.reply:
Not quite—sellers can't just pick any price and expect buyers to pay it. Both buyers and sellers influence the price. If sellers set the price too high, buyers won't buy enough, and if it's too low, sellers may not want to sell.

If sellers set the price much higher than buyers are willing to pay, what would you expect to see in stores?

turns.learner: it depends on people?
turns.reply:
If sellers set the price higher than buyers want to pay, stores end up with extra goods (a surplus). Sellers then lower the price to get rid of the surplus. If the price is too low, there aren't enough goods for everyone (a shortage), so buyers compete and prices go up.

Why do you think a shortage makes prices rise?

turns.learner: If more people want it than there is, the price goes up.
turns.reply:
Exactly. When more people want something than there is available (a shortage), buyers compete, so sellers can raise the price.

What do you think would happen if the price stayed below the equilibrium for a long time?

turns.learner: continue
turns.reply:
The market naturally adjusts when prices are too high or too low: shortages push prices up, and surpluses push prices down, until the market reaches equilibrium.

If a new video game console comes out and sells out everywhere, what do you think happens to its price on resale markets?

turns.learner: ok
turns.reply: Here's a quick summary of how supply and demand set price. Can you explain in your own words how this process works?

turns.learner: The price settles where the amount people want equals the amount sold.
turns.reply: Right—the price settles where the amount people want to buy equals the amount sellers offer. Now, tell me: if there is a surplus of a product, what happens to the price?
